narrative:
The model determined that you have a 51.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your first-year grades had the strongest influence. You placed in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of sixth decile among accepted students. This low ranking strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your third-year class ranking was the next most important factor; finishing in the second decile again pulled the prediction toward not passing. Your LSAT score was the third key driver. At 33.5, it sits noticeably below the 37.2 average of accepted students and therefore worked in the opposite direction, modestly increasing the chance you would pass.

Taken together, the two weak academic rankings outweighed the positive effect of your LSAT and tipped the model past the acceptance threshold.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record. Retaking courses to improve your GPA, preparing intensively for a higher LSAT score, or gaining structured study support for the bar exam would directly address the factors that led to this decision. Many students in similar situations have successfully re-applied after showing clear improvement in these areas.
